title: The Buddha at the lunch table
hookLine: Sam calls the Buddha a Hindu god, and Dawa goes quiet
carry: honor him as vishnu's form; his story is theirs
tomorrow: Dawa asks which ten forms Priya counts. why do the lists differ?

lines: THE LOUD TABLE BY THE WINDOW.
cards: Thursday, the loud table by the cafeteria window. Sam has spent a week living at Priya's house and has picked up a lot, and wants to share it. Guess what, Sam announces, the Buddha is a Hindu god.
Vishnu in another form. Across the table, Dawa, who is Buddhist, puts her fork down and goes quiet. Sam looks at Priya.
Priya looks at her tray. Everyone is waiting for her, because she's supposed to be the one who knows.

teach.h: AVATARA: GOD COMES DOWN, FORM AFTER FORM.
teach.b: The honest answer comes in two halves. The first half is the Hindu tellings, and they rest on a big Hindu idea: avatara, God coming down.
Vishnu, Hindus say, descends in form after form whenever the world needs him, so Hindu poets could look at a great teacher of compassion and see Vishnu's face.
The Bhagavata names the Buddha in Vishnu's line, at the start of the Kali age.

teach.h: THE HINDU HALF: VISHNU WITH A COMPASSIONATE HEART.
teach.b: Jayadeva sings him as Vishnu with a compassionate heart, who out of pity faulted sacrifices that killed animals. Some lists leave him out and count Balarama in his place. Hindus have kept all of these.

The second half belongs to Dawa. The Buddha's own followers tell of a man who left home looking for an end to suffering, sat down in meditation, and woke up, and then spent his life teaching the way he'd found.
In that telling he isn't Vishnu's descent at all.
He is the Buddha in his own right, their teacher.

teach.h: HALF A STORY, TOLD AS WHOLE.
teach.b: So Sam's sentence is half a story told as if it were the whole.
Here's the Hindu lesson inside it: seeing God's face in another tradition's teacher is a way Hindus honor, and honoring isn't owning.

The fair version goes like this: some Hindu texts tell him as a descent of Vishnu; Buddhists tell his story another way, and it's theirs to tell. Priya says it, more or less like that. Dawa picks her fork back up.
Then she asks Priya a question of her own.

how: Hindu teachers who speak of the Buddha as an avatar often add that Buddhists tell his life in their own scriptures; in interfaith settings people name whose telling they're giving.

o: told by Hindus as Vishnu, by Buddhists as their teacher
a Hindu god whom Buddhists later took from Vishnu
a title for any teacher who studies the Vedas

games.q: who tells it how — tap the pairs.
p: their own teacher, the Awakened One

s: Hindu texts agree on one meaning for the Buddha
the Bhagavata, Jayadeva, and the lists that leave him out all differ.
Buddhists tell of a man who left home seeking an end to suffering, and awoke
in their telling he is their teacher in his own right.
saying 'as the tradition tells it' means the story isn't true
it marks whose telling you're hearing; it doesn't decide who's right.

games.q: Dawa asks: so what do you know about how we tell his story? what's a fair one-line version?
o: a man left home to find an end to suffering, woke up, and taught the way.
Vishnu came down as a prince to bewilder the enemies of the gods.
a sage moved by animals at the altar, who praised the Vedic sacrifice.
games.why: that's the Buddhist telling, in one line. The second is the Bhagavata's verse, and the third gets Jayadeva backwards: his Buddha faults the sacrifice.

practice: Bring to mind three people who once told you their own story in their own words: a grandparent, a friend, someone you barely knew. Count them on your fingers, one slow breath for each.
Then rest for the sit with the thanks you'd give each of them.

wordCard.voice: Buddha: in some Hindu texts, a descent of Vishnu; to Buddhists, their own teacher, the Awakened One, whose story is theirs to tell.

carryVoice: Your line: honor him as Vishnu's form; his story is theirs. Avatara is a way to honor, not to own. Until tomorrow, then.

sources.ref: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, canto 1, the hymn of the ten forms (looked back to)
